prompts: This is an instructional notebook. It introduces feature scaling with StandardScaler and the scikit-learn Pipeline abstraction, demonstrating how preprocessing and model training can be chained and why scaling benefits gradient-based models. Key learning objectives are: (1) understanding why scaling is needed — it equalizes feature ranges for distance-based models and speeds up gradient-descent convergence for linear models; (2) learning the transformer API: fit computes mean_ and scale_, transform applies standardization, and fit_transform does both; (3) using make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()) to chain steps, fitting and predicting with the same interface as a standalone model; (4) comparing scaled vs. unscaled LogisticRegression to observe that scaling reduces iterations from 60 to 9 and fitting time by roughly half, with no change in test accuracy (~0.807). Expected outputs include: data_train_scaled with near-zero means and unit standard deviations, model.named_steps showing 'standardscaler' and 'logisticregression', and the printed accuracy/timing/iteration summary for both pipelines. The trailing underscore convention in scikit-learn (e.g. mean_, scale_, n_iter_) marks attributes that are learned from data during fit, not set by the user. n_iter_ is an array (one value per target class in multiclass settings, or a single-element array for binary); accessing n_iter_[0] retrieves the iteration count for the first (or only) class. If a ConvergenceWarning appears, the recommended fix is to scale the data first rather than simply increasing max_iter. If asked about more information on the dataset, refer to https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/datasets_adult_census.html
